notes.1: This proved to be a good starting question with the majority of candidates obtaining full marks. There were however several serious misunderstandings about the term “perpendicular bisector”. A significant number of candidates failed to realise that the perpendicular bisector was a line passing through the midpoint of the line joining the two points and at right angles to this line. Other errors were to assume that the gradient was the x-step divided by the y-step or to assume that the midpoint was (½(x −x ,½(y −y ). Answer: (3½, 0)
notes.2: This was generally well answered, though arithmetic errors in dealing with (−4)², (−4)³, (½)³ and (½)4 were widespread. It was common to see the minus sign omitted throughout and a final answer of “15 + 160” instead of “15 – 160” was often offered. A significant number of candidates failed to realise that two terms in the expansion of   were needed to find the coefficient of x². Answer: −145
notes.3a: Most candidates realised the need to use sin²θ = 1 – k², but only a few realised that, because θ was reflex, the negative square root needed to be taken.
notes.3ii: Only a small number of correct solutions was seen. Candidates failed to realise that because θ was reflex, and cosθ > 0, then 270º < θ < 360º and that therefore 540º < 2θ < 720º leading to sin2θ < 0. A few attempts were seen using the double angle formulae for sin2θ, but again these were usually incomplete through failure to realise that because sinθ < 0 and cosθ > 0, sin2θ < 0.
notes.4i: This was often badly answered, depending at which stage candidates used the substitution θ = psinθ. Candidates starting with ½r²sinθ = ½r²θ − ½r²sinθ or r²sinθ = ½r²θ invariably obtained the correct value of p. Unfortunately many made the substitution at an early stage and were unable to obtain a value of p because of errors such as ½r²sin(psinθ) = ½r²psin²θ. Many candidates opted to use the formula “½×base×height” for the area of a triangle and this led to expressions containing sine or cosine of “½θ”, from which there was usually no recovery.
notes.4ii: Most candidates correctly evaluated the arc length AXB. Although there were many correct solutions for the perimeter, common errors were writing AB as 2×8×sin2.4; forgetting to multiply 8sin1.2 by 2; and premature approximation leading to 34.2.
notes.5i: It was pleasing to see many perfectly correct solutions. Most candidates added the fractions sin2θ+sinθ correctly and used “sin²θ + cos²θ = 1” to obtain the fraction . At least a third of all cosθ(1+sinθ) candidates did not manage to factorise this to give and then to deduce the answer. Some very good candidates failed to make this last step and it was impossible to give the final 2 marks. Candidates must realise the need to show all working and explanations in this type of question.
notes.6i: Most candidates recognised that 8r = 8 + 8d and that 8r2 = 8 + 20d, though common errors were to misinterpret arithmetic for geometric or to assume incorrectly that the nth term of a geometric progression is arn. Elimination of r or d caused many candidates considerable difficulty and was often accompanied by a mass of algebra. Use of = as a starting point generally 8+8d 8+20d led to correct values for d and then r.

notes.7ii: This was rarely correct and often not attempted. Only about a third of all candidates realised the   need to find the unit vector in the direction of BA and then multiply this by 12 to find CC .DD . Many candidates thought that CD was the position vector of D.
notes.8: Most candidates realised the need to integrate twice and the standard of integration was good. Unfortunately, failure to include a constant of integration (either once or twice) meant that most of the marks were unavailable. Some candidates used the same letter for both integrations. About a half of all candidates, whilst attempting to use y = −10 when x = 3, failed to realise that = 0 when x = 3. Answer: (−2, 105)
notes.10i: This part was extremely well answered with candidates coping comfortably with the composite function. Occasionally ff was given as 2(2x – 3) instead of 2(2x – 3) – 3.
notes.10iv: As in part (i), most candidates coped well with finding gf, though “(2x – 3)² + 4x” was a common incorrect expression. Virtually all candidates realised the need to use the discriminant (b² − 4ac) but a significant number of solutions were seen in which “= p” was only introduced after the discriminant had been used.
notes.10v: Only a small proportion of candidates realised that the smallest value of k was −2, the value at which the curve had a minimum point.
notes.10vi: This was very well answered, with most candidates realising the need to use “completing the square” to express x in terms of y. Marks were lost through failing to remove the ± in the answer or to leave the answer as a function of y instead of x.
notes.key_messages: Teachers should reinforce with all their candidates the need for full presentation of working, especially in questions where candidates are asked to prove a particular result. If necessary steps of working are omitted then full marks cannot be awarded. This applied particularly to Question 5 where often very good candidates failed to show sufficient working. Whilst Examiners will generally accept steps that can be done mentally or on a calculator, this does not apply to questions that require a rigorous proof. notes.general_comments: General comments While presentation of work for many candidates was satisfactory there were significant numbers of candidates whose work was untidy and difficult to follow. The rubric on the front of the Question Paper says ‘You are reminded of the need for clear presentation in your answers’. It is generally true that marks cannot be awarded if methods used are not clear. It is worth noting here a very common error: forgetting the ± sign. For example, in Question 8(ii), p² = 4  p = ±2. Mistakes of this kind were also seen in Questions 2(ii), 7, 9(i). Comments on specific questions
